items.said: “If you can’t show a piece of paper, too bad.”
items.q: Does a service dog need papers, an ID card, or a certificate?
answer: No. Federal law has no ID, license, or certificate for service dogs, and a business can’t ask for one. The only check allowed is the two questions.
Cards and certificates sold online carry no legal weight. Anyone can buy one, so they prove nothing either way.

items.said: “There should be a registry, like a medical alert bracelet.”
items.q: Is there an official service dog registry?
answer: No. There is no government registry in the U.S. Sites that sell “registration” are private businesses, not the government.

When the Justice Department wrote the rules, it chose not to require certification. Many service dogs are trained by their owners, and professionally trained dogs can cost tens of thousands of dollars. Changing this would take a new law from Congress.

items.said: “So it’s all word-based? Would they have to prove it in court?”
items.q: Does a handler ever have to prove the dog is a service dog?
answer: Not at the door. In a lawsuit, yes. The person suing has to show they have a disability and that the dog is trained to do a task for it. Courts look at evidence such as training history and testimony.
So the two questions are a quick screen for staff, and a lawsuit is where the facts actually get tested.

items.said: “Real service dogs should be microchipped and scannable.”
items.q: Can a microchip, vest, or tag prove a dog is a service dog?
answer: No. No chip, tag, vest, or app is legally recognized as proof. A dog’s microchip only links it to an owner.

items.said: “People faking it ruin it for everyone.”
items.q: Is it illegal to pass off a pet as a service dog?
answer: In most states, yes. As of September 2026, 33 states, including Arizona, penalize passing off a pet as a service animal in public places, usually with a fine or a misdemeanor. A few more penalize it only in housing. Pick your state at the top of the Home screen to see its rule.
Federal law has no penalty for this, which is why state laws matter.

items.said: “It’s private property. He can refuse service to anyone.”
items.q: Can a business refuse service to anyone it wants?
answer: Not for a reason the law protects. Stores, restaurants, hotels, and other private businesses open to the public are covered by the ADA. They can’t turn someone away because of a disability or because of their service dog.
A business can still refuse service for a reason unrelated to disability, such as a dress code applied to every customer. It can’t use a reason like that as cover for removing the dog.

items.said: “Just say you’re closing early and she can be on her way.”
items.q: Can staff make up an excuse to get a handler to leave?
answer: No. A made-up reason used to remove someone because of their dog is still disability discrimination. If the store stays open for other customers, that’s strong evidence in a complaint.

items.said: “It’s a concert. No dogs allowed, period.”
items.q: Can a concert, stadium, or festival ban service dogs?
answer: No. Concert venues, arenas, stadiums, theaters, fairs, and festivals must allow service dogs in areas open to the public, even when they have a “no pets” rule. That includes events on government property, such as county fairgrounds.

They can’t charge for the dog, seat you apart, or require you to call ahead. They can remove a dog that is out of control, such as one that barks repeatedly through a show, and they can keep dogs out of animal exhibits where the animals are natural prey or predators of dogs.

items.said: “What about people who are allergic or afraid of dogs?”
items.q: What if a customer or employee is allergic to or afraid of dogs?
answer: Allergies and fear aren’t valid reasons to deny access. When both people need to be in the same space, the business should try to separate them, for example by seating them in different parts of the room.

items.said: “What happened to the manager after?”
items.q: What can happen to a business that wrongly refuses a service dog?
answer: The handler can file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Justice or a state civil rights office, or sue. Under federal law, a private lawsuit can force the business to change its policy and pay the handler’s legal fees. The Justice Department can also seek civil penalties.
Some states, including Arizona, have their own disability laws with additional remedies.

items.said: “Under the ADA, service dogs must be leashed.”
items.q: Does a service dog have to be on a leash?
answer: Yes, a service dog must be leashed, harnessed, or tethered in public. The exceptions are when a leash would get in the way of the dog’s task, or the handler’s disability prevents using one.
In those cases, the dog still has to be under voice or signal control. A business can ask the handler to get an out-of-control dog under control.

items.said: “It was pulling and barking and misbehaving.”
items.q: Can a business remove a service dog that misbehaves?
answer: Yes, if the dog is out of control and the handler doesn’t take effective action, or if the dog isn’t housebroken. Repeated barking, lunging, or wandering off can count. A single bark or a quick correction usually doesn’t.
The person must still be offered service without the dog.

items.said: “Why didn’t the dog alert? She had to tell it what to do.”
items.q: If the dog didn’t alert, or the handler gave it a command, is it fake?
answer: Not necessarily. Many tasks start with a cue from the handler, such as bracing, retrieving medication, or blocking. Not every service dog does alert work. Dogs can also miss an alert, the same way any medical device isn’t perfect.

Symptoms also vary a lot from person to person. Someone having a POTS, anxiety, or fainting episode may still be able to talk, or may not look sick at all. Staff aren’t allowed to judge a disability by how someone looks or acts.
Staff can’t ask for a demonstration. What matters at the door is the answer to the two questions and whether the dog is under control.

items.said: “Pets riding in purses and shopping carts.”
items.q: Can a service dog ride in a shopping cart?
answer: The ADA doesn’t address carts directly. Service dogs generally walk on the floor, and food-safety rules make carts a poor place for any dog. A handler may carry a small dog if that’s part of how it works.

items.said: “Isn’t asking about my condition a HIPAA violation?”
items.q: Does HIPAA stop a business from asking about my disability?
answer: No. HIPAA only applies to doctors, hospitals, pharmacies, health insurers, and companies that handle health records for them. It doesn’t apply to a store clerk or restaurant manager.
The rule that protects your privacy at a business is the ADA. Under the ADA, staff may ask only:

**1.** Is the dog a service animal required because of a disability?
**2.** What work or task has the dog been trained to perform?

Staff may not ask what your disability or diagnosis is, ask for medical records or a doctor’s note, ask to see the dog perform its task, or ask either question when the dog’s role is obvious, such as a guide dog leading a blind person.
You can answer the second question by naming the task, such as “he alerts me before a medical episode,” without naming your condition.

items.said: “POTS isn’t on the Social Security disability list.”
items.q: Does a condition have to be on the Social Security list to count?
answer: No. The ADA’s definition of disability is much broader than Social Security’s. A condition counts if it substantially limits a major life activity, such as walking, standing, or the heart and circulatory system.
Conditions that come and go, like POTS, epilepsy, or diabetes, count when they are active. Congress added that in 2008.

items.said: “Emotional support animals have no place in that category.”
items.q: Is an emotional support animal a service dog?
answer: No. A dog that provides comfort just by being there isn’t a service dog under the ADA and has no right to enter stores or restaurants.
A psychiatric service dog is different. If it’s trained to do a specific task, such as interrupting a panic attack, it’s a service dog.

items.said: “I can’t afford $10,000 for a trained dog.”
items.q: Does a service dog have to be professionally trained?
answer: No. The ADA doesn’t require professional training. Owner-trained dogs have the same rights, as long as the dog is trained to do a task and behaves in public.

items.said: “Just vest your dog and keep it on a leash to avoid all this.”
items.q: What can handlers do to avoid confrontations?
answer: A vest isn’t required, but many handlers find it cuts down on questions. Keeping the dog leashed is required in most cases.

If you’re challenged, stay calm. Answer the two questions and show the staff screen in this app. If staff still refuse, leave, then write down names, the time, and what was said in the Log tab while it’s fresh.

items.said: “A service dog in training has the same rights in most states.”
items.q: Do service dogs in training have access rights?
answer: Not under federal law. Many states give them access, often only when they’re with a trainer. Arizona gives dogs in training the same access as trained service dogs. Check your state in the selector at the top.

items.said: “Why sit there and argue? You’re making a scene.”
items.q: What should I do if a business refuses my service dog?
answer: Arguing rarely changes a manager’s mind in the moment, and it can make a medical episode worse. These steps protect both your health and your case:

**1. Stay calm.** Answer the two questions, briefly.
**2. Show the staff screen** in this app. Many refusals end here.
**3. Ask for a manager,** or the company’s corporate or customer service number.
**4. If they still refuse, leave.** Staying after being told to go can lead to a trespassing complaint, even if the business was wrong.
**5. Write it all down** in the Log tab: names, time, what was said, and any witnesses.
**6. File a complaint** with the business’s corporate office, the Justice Department, or your state civil rights office.
Taking care of yourself first is not giving up your rights. The complaint is where the business is held responsible.

items.said: “Always recording too.”
items.q: Can I record the conversation on my phone?
answer: Often, yes, but it depends on your state. Most states, including Arizona, let you record a conversation you’re part of. About a dozen states, including California, Florida, and Washington, require everyone’s consent to record a private conversation.

Video in a public area of a store is usually allowed, but a business can set its own no-filming rule for its property. A recording helps most as evidence for a complaint, not as something to argue with in the moment. Be careful about posting it online.

items.said: “Call the cops and have her arrested for trespassing.”
items.q: Can the police remove a handler with a service dog?
answer: Police respond to a trespass call like any other. They usually aren’t there to decide an ADA dispute on the spot. A handler who refuses to leave after being told to go can risk a trespass charge.

But calling the police doesn’t make the business right. If the refusal broke the ADA, the handler can still file a complaint or sue. In some states, such as Illinois and Ohio, denying a service dog access is itself a crime, and police can act against the business. Check your state card on the Home tab.
Police departments are also covered by the ADA, and the Justice Department publishes guidance for officers on the same two-question rule.

items.said: “Now she can file a pain and suffering lawsuit.” “She’ll own that store.”
items.q: Can a handler sue for money?
answer: Under the federal ADA, usually not. In a private lawsuit over a store or restaurant, a court can order the business to change its policies and pay the handler’s attorney fees, but it can’t award money for pain and suffering. The Justice Department can seek civil penalties.

Some state laws do allow money. California’s Unruh Act, for example, allows at least $4,000 per violation. Refusals by employers, landlords, and government agencies are covered by other laws, which can also allow damages.

items.said: “If he saw the dog misbehave, he can ask them to leave.”
items.q: What should staff do when they doubt a service dog?
answer: This is the safe, legal way for staff to handle it:

**1. Don’t judge by looks.** No vest, a small breed, or casual clothes doesn’t mean the dog is fake.
**2. Ask the two questions,** only if the dog’s task isn’t obvious. Accept the answers.
**3. Watch behavior, not paperwork.** Lunging, repeated barking, begging at tables, jumping on people, or an accident on the floor are real problems.
**4. If the dog is out of control,** ask the handler to get it under control. If that doesn’t work, ask that the dog leave.
**5. Offer to serve the person without the dog,** such as finishing the order while the dog waits outside with someone.
**6. Never make up an excuse,** like “we’re closing,” to get rid of a handler.
Following these steps protects the business from a complaint and from fake service dogs at the same time.

items.said: “Begging at tables, a dog pooped in the dining room, two dogs attacked each other.”
items.q: What behavior can get a service dog removed?
answer: Service dogs are trained to ignore food, people, and other animals, and to stay quiet and close. A business can remove a dog that is out of control and not corrected, or that isn’t housebroken. Examples include:

• Growling, lunging, snapping, or biting
• Fighting with or chasing another animal
• Relieving itself indoors
• Repeated barking in a quiet place
• Begging, sniffing, or taking food from tables or shelves
• Jumping on people or wandering away from the handler
Each dog is judged on its own behavior. A business can’t ban all service dogs because a different dog behaved badly.

items.said: “The ADA says one thing, but our state law says another.”
items.q: What if state law and federal law say different things?
answer: The law that protects the person with a disability more is the one that applies. The ADA sets the minimum everywhere in the U.S., including the territories. A state can add rights, such as access for dogs in training, but it can’t take away ADA rights.
So if a state law requires a service dog ID or vest, a business still can’t demand one at the door, because the ADA doesn’t allow it.

items.said: “She’s just a kid. Who’s in charge of the dog?”
items.q: Can a child or teenager have a service dog?
answer: Yes. The ADA sets no minimum age. In public, the child or a parent or other adult with them can handle the dog, as long as the dog stays under control.

Businesses follow the same two-question rule. They can ask the child or the adult. At school, the school may need to give a student some help handling the dog, but staff don’t have to care for it. The Justice Department has sued schools that required families to hire a separate adult handler.
See Children and teens in the More tab for school tips.
items.cite: DOJ ADA Service Animal FAQ Q27

items.said: “You don’t need a dog for a mental illness.” “Everyone has anxiety.”
items.q: Can anxiety or PTSD qualify someone for a service dog?
answer: Yes, if the condition is serious enough to be a disability and the dog is trained to do a task for it. The ADA covers mental health conditions the same way it covers physical ones. Everyday worry isn’t a disability. Severe PTSD, panic disorder, or bipolar disorder can be.

The key is the task. A dog trained to interrupt panic attacks, wake someone from nightmares, or create space in crowds is a service dog. A dog that only provides comfort is an emotional support animal, with no public access rights.
